title: Defective product or refused refund
sample_questions: I bought a phone that stopped working in a week and the shop refuses a refund.
What can I do about a faulty product?
explanation: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, you can ask for a repair, replacement, refund or compensation if a product or service is defective, or if the seller cheated or misled you.
rights: Right to safe goods and services.
Right to correct information about price, quality and quantity.
Right to repair, replacement, refund or compensation.
Right to be heard and to file a complaint, with or without a lawyer.
next_steps: Keep the bill, warranty card, photos and chat messages.
Write to the seller or company, state the problem and ask for a remedy by a fixed date.
Call the National Consumer Helpline (1915) for help in settling it.
If unresolved, file a complaint with the District Consumer Commission, online through e-Daakhil. Complaints are usually filed within 2 years.
professional: For high-value or complicated disputes, talk to a consumer lawyer or a legal aid clinic. Small complaints can be filed on your own.

title: Employee rights: unpaid salary and unfair dismissal
sample_questions: My employer has not paid my salary for two months.
Can my company fire me without notice?
explanation: Employers must pay agreed wages on time, follow minimum wage rules and deduct only what the law allows. India's labour laws are being merged into new Labour Codes, so which rule applies can depend on your state, job and employer size.
rights: Right to wages on time and not less than the minimum wage.
Right to the terms of your job in writing, such as an appointment letter.
Provident fund and ESI benefits where they apply.
Right to a safe workplace, free from sexual harassment.
next_steps: Collect your appointment letter, salary slips, bank statements and messages.
Write to your employer (email is fine) asking for the dues by a fixed date.
If it is ignored, complain to the Labour Commissioner or labour office of your district.
Ask your state or district legal services authority for free help.
professional: Talk to a labour lawyer or union representative if you have been dismissed, if the dues are large, or if the employer threatens you.

title: Tenant and landlord problems
sample_questions: My landlord is not returning my security deposit.
Can my landlord throw me out without notice?
explanation: Rent and eviction rules differ from state to state. In general, a landlord cannot force a tenant out, lock them out or cut off water or electricity without following the legal process.
rights: Right to a written rent agreement with clear terms.
Right to proper notice and a legal process before eviction.
Right to essential services such as water and electricity.
Right to claim back the security deposit, after fair deductions.
next_steps: Keep the rent agreement, rent receipts and proof of deposit payment.
Send the landlord a written request (or legal notice) to return the deposit by a fixed date.
Do not sign anything you do not understand when leaving.
If it is not resolved, approach the Rent Authority or civil court, or try mediation or a Lok Adalat.
professional: Speak to a property lawyer or legal aid clinic if you face eviction, lock-out or a large unpaid deposit.

sources.label: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (Model Tenancy Act)

title: Borrowed money not returned
sample_questions: I lent money to a friend and he is not returning it.
My cheque from someone bounced. What now?
explanation: If someone does not repay money you lent, you can send a written demand, then go to a civil court to recover it. A bounced cheque can also lead to a case under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
rights: Right to ask for repayment and to take the matter to court.
Right to try mediation or a Lok Adalat for a faster, cheaper settlement.
next_steps: Collect proof: messages, bank transfers, receipts, written promises, cheques.
Send a polite written demand, then a legal notice if needed.
For a bounced cheque, the notice usually has to be sent within 30 days of the bank's return memo. Check exact deadlines with a lawyer.
Money recovery cases generally must be filed within 3 years, so do not wait too long.
professional: Get a lawyer or legal aid for a legal notice or court case. Deadlines are strict, especially for cheque cases.

title: Free legal aid
sample_questions: I cannot afford a lawyer. Where can I get free legal help?
Who is eligible for free legal aid?
explanation: Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, certain people can get a free lawyer and free legal advice from the National, State and District Legal Services Authorities.
rights: Eligible groups include women, children, persons with disabilities, SC/ST members, persons in custody, victims of trafficking and people below an income limit set by the state.
Free legal aid is part of the constitutional promise of equal justice (Article 39A).
next_steps: Call the NALSA helpline 15100.
Visit the District Legal Services Authority, usually in the district court complex.
Try Tele-Law for free advice through a Common Service Centre.
Lok Adalats settle many disputes without court fees.
professional: A legal aid lawyer is a professional. Ask the authority to assign one for your case.

title: Online fraud and cybercrime
sample_questions: Someone took money from my account using a fake link.
I was cheated through a UPI scam. What should I do?
explanation: Online fraud should be reported as fast as possible. Quick reporting gives the bank and police the best chance to freeze the money and may limit your loss under bank rules.
rights: Right to report cybercrime online or at any police station.
Right to ask your bank to investigate an unauthorised transaction.
Right to have intimate or abusive content reported for removal.
next_steps: Call 1930 (cyber fraud helpline) right away, then report at cybercrime.gov.in.
Inform your bank immediately and block the card, UPI or account.
Keep screenshots, transaction IDs, phone numbers and links. Do not delete anything.
Change passwords and never share OTP, PIN or CVV with anyone.
professional: If you lost a large amount or were blackmailed, also file a police complaint and consider talking to a cyber-law lawyer.

title: Domestic violence
sample_questions: My husband beats me. What can I do?
My in-laws are harassing me for dowry.
explanation: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 protects women from physical, emotional, sexual and economic abuse at home. You can get help even if you do not want to leave your home.
rights: Right to live in the shared home.
Right to a protection order that stops the abuser from contacting or harming you.
Right to maintenance, and to custody of your children in some cases.
Right to free legal aid.
next_steps: If you are in danger now, call 112. The women's helpline is 181.
Go to a safe place, such as a relative's home or a One Stop Centre.
Contact a Protection Officer or the District Legal Services Authority.
Keep records of injuries, messages and medical reports if it is safe to do so.
professional: Please speak to a lawyer, Protection Officer or women's support organisation. Your safety comes first.

sources.label: Ministry of Women and Child Development

title: Children's rights and child safety
sample_questions: A school is refusing admission to my child.
A child I know is being made to work or is being hurt.
explanation: Children have the right to free education, protection from abuse and protection from harmful work. The Right to Education Act, 2009, the POCSO Act, 2012 and child labour laws protect them.
rights: Free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14.
Protection from sexual abuse and exploitation under POCSO.
Children are not allowed to do hazardous work, and young children are not allowed to work.
Right to be heard and to be safe at home, at school and in public.
next_steps: If a child is in danger or being abused, call CHILDLINE 1098 or 112.
For school admission problems, write to the school and then to the Block or District Education Officer.
Keep records, such as dates, names and messages.
Under POCSO, reporting suspected abuse is a duty.
professional: Contact CHILDLINE, the Child Welfare Committee or a legal aid lawyer for serious cases.

title: Your rights when arrested
sample_questions: What are my rights if the police arrest me?
Police have taken my brother to the station. What can we do?
explanation: The Constitution (Article 22) and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 give every arrested person basic protections. The police cannot hold you without telling you why.
rights: Right to be told the reason for the arrest.
Right to inform a relative or friend, and to meet a lawyer.
Right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.
Right to remain silent and not to be forced to confess.
Right to a free lawyer if you cannot afford one.
Women should generally not be arrested between sunset and sunrise without a magistrate's permission.
next_steps: Stay calm and do not sign blank or unread papers.
Ask for the reason for arrest, and note the names of the officers.
Say clearly that you want a lawyer, or ask for a legal aid lawyer.
Tell the magistrate about any ill-treatment. Family members can call 112 or NALSA 15100.
professional: Contact a criminal lawyer or the legal aid lawyer at the court as soon as possible.

title: Filing an FIR or police complaint
sample_questions: The police are refusing to register my FIR.
How do I file a police complaint?
explanation: If a serious (cognisable) offence is reported, the police must register an FIR. You can file it at any police station, even if the crime happened elsewhere. This is called a Zero FIR.
rights: Right to a free copy of the FIR.
Right to have a serious crime recorded as an FIR.
Right to a Zero FIR at any police station.
next_steps: Write down what happened with dates, places and names.
If the station refuses, send your complaint in writing to the Superintendent of Police.
You can also approach a magistrate or use your state police's online complaint portal.
Ask for the FIR number and a free copy.
professional: If the police keep refusing, a lawyer or legal aid authority can help you approach the magistrate.

title: Right to Information (RTI)
sample_questions: How can I find out the status of my pending government application?
How do I file an RTI?
explanation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 lets any citizen ask a government office for information. The office must normally reply within 30 days.
rights: Right to ask for records and information held by public authorities.
Right to a reply, or to a written reason if information is refused.
Right to appeal if there is no reply.
next_steps: Write a short application stating exactly what you want to know.
Pay the small application fee (it is waived for below-poverty-line applicants).
File it online at the RTI portal or by post to the Public Information Officer.
If there is no reply, make a first appeal, then a second appeal to the Information Commission.
professional: A lawyer is not required. Legal aid volunteers can help with drafting.
